name: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases

clinicalPearls: FMF is the prototype hereditary autoinflammatory disease: recurrent self-limited fever with serosal, synovial, or cutaneous inflammation, distinguished from autoimmune disease by the relative absence of high-titer autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells and a predominant role of the innate immune system (Harrison 22e p.2934).
Roughly 90% of patients have their first attack by age 20; typical episodes last about 24-72 hours, with arthritic attacks tending to run longer (Harrison 22e p.2934).
Over 90% of FMF patients have abdominal (peritoneal) attacks; laparotomy reveals a sterile neutrophil-rich peritoneal exudate, and ascites is rare (Harrison 22e p.2934).

Erysipelas-like erythema, a raised erythematous rash typically on the dorsum of the foot, ankle, or lower leg, is the most characteristic skin finding and occurs most often in M694V homozygotes (Harrison 22e p.2934).

FMF arthritis is usually monoarticular (knee, ankle, hip) with large sterile neutrophil-rich effusions and little erythema or warmth; radiographic changes are rare even after repeated attacks (Harrison 22e p.2934).

The MEFV gene encodes pyrin (~95 kDa); its N-terminal PYRIN domain nucleates the pyrin inflammasome that activates caspase-1, driving IL-1beta and IL-18 secretion and gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis (Harrison 22e p.2934).

FMF-associated MEFV mutations are gain-of-function, lowering the threshold for pyrin inflammasome activation; severe disease-associated mutations cluster in exon 10, and M694V homozygosity predicts earlier onset and more arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2935-2936).

The principal hereditary recurrent fever syndromes are differentiated by attack length, ethnicity, and features: TRAPS (TNFRSF1A, dominant, attacks often >7 days, migratory myalgia with overlying erythema, periorbital edema/conjunctivitis), HIDS/MKD (MVK, recessive, painful cervical adenopathy and oral ulcers), and the NLRP3-associated cryopyrinopathies FCAS, MWS, and NOMID (Harrison 22e p.2935-2937).

Cryopyrinopathies form a spectrum: FCAS (cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fever, arthralgia, conjunctivitis), MWS (urticarial rash not cold-induced, progressive sensorineural hearing loss), and NOMID/neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (chronic aseptic meningitis, characteristic arthropathy, rash) (Harrison 22e p.2937).

About one-third of clinically typical NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations but are mosaic for somatic NLRP3 mutations; somatic NLRP3 mosaicism has rarely been reported in Schnitzler's syndrome (middle-age recurrent fever, urticaria, monoclonal IgM gammopathy, abnormal bone remodeling) (Harrison 22e p.2936-2937).

PFAPA (periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, cervical adenitis) is the most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, notable for clock-like regularity, familial but non-Mendelian clustering, and a tendency to resolve by early adulthood (Harrison 22e p.2937).

Over 60 monogenic autoinflammatory diseases are now recognized, grouped mechanistically into inflammasomopathies (FMF, HIDS, CAPS, PAPA, NLRC4-related), type I interferonopathies (STING-associated vasculopathy, COPA syndrome, Aicardi-Goutieres, CANDLE), and relopathies affecting NF-kB / TNF-induced cell death (Harrison 22e p.2937).
harrison.pathophysiology: These disorders reflect dysregulated innate immunity rather than adaptive autoimmunity. In FMF, gain-of-function MEFV mutations lower the activation threshold of the pyrin inflammasome; pyrin (via its PYRIN domain and an adaptor) assembles a macromolecular complex that activates caspase-1, producing IL-1beta and IL-18 and triggering gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis. Pyrin normally senses bacterial toxins that inactivate RhoA GTPase as part of host defense. The other syndromes map to specific innate pathways: TRAPS arises from misfolding, aggregation, and retention of mutant TNFR1 with ligand-independent kinase activation, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokine release; HIDS/MKD results from mevalonate kinase deficiency that impairs isoprenoid (geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate) synthesis, mislocalizing and inactivating RhoA and thereby activating the pyrin inflammasome; FCAS/MWS/NOMID arise from NLRP3 (cryopyrin) mutations forming an overactive NLRP3 inflammasome with excess IL-1beta and IL-18. Broader categories include interferonopathies driven by aberrant intracellular nucleic-acid sensing (excess type I interferon) and relopathies that dysregulate NF-kB activation or TNF-induced cell death. Untreated chronic inflammation can lead to systemic AA amyloidosis from deposition of a serum amyloid A fragment.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary recurrent fever syndromes (TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, FCAS, MWS, NOMID)
Systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis / adult Still's disease
Gynecologic disorders (in women presenting with recurrent abdominal pain)
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis / adult Still's disease
additionalInvestigations: MEFV genetic testing (severe mutations cluster in exon 10; ~70% of clinically typical FMF have two mutations in trans; expert-curated mutation databases such as Infevers aid interpretation)
Acute-phase markers during attacks: elevated ESR, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis (in children), and raised C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, and serum immunoglobulins
Urinalysis (transient albuminuria/hematuria during attacks; persistent proteinuria between attacks should raise concern for amyloidosis)
Renal or rectal biopsy to confirm suspected AA amyloidosis

Genotype-specific testing for other syndromes: TNFRSF1A (TRAPS), MVK with markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks (HIDS/MKD), NLRP3 (cryopyrinopathies, including testing for somatic mosaicism)
Imaging during attacks: chest radiograph (atelectasis/effusion in pleural attacks), upright abdominal radiograph or CT (air-fluid levels, small amount of free fluid)
redFlags: Persistent proteinuria between attacks, suggesting developing AA amyloidosis
Severe hyperpyrexia or febrile seizures in infants
Protracted febrile myalgia lasting several weeks
In cryopyrinopathies, sensorineural hearing loss (MWS) or chronic aseptic meningitis and progressive visual/CNS involvement (NOMID)
Features of secondary vasculitis (IgA vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa) occurring at increased frequency in FMF
Adult-onset relapsing polychondritis, Sweet's syndrome, vasculitis, or myelodysplasia in older men suggesting VEXAS syndrome
harrison.prognosis: FMF attacks are self-limited and recur with variable frequency over a lifetime; episodes may even be associated with remission during pregnancy. The major determinant of long-term outcome is systemic AA amyloidosis, historically a common and serious complication. Amyloidosis risk is increased by the M694V homozygous genotype, positive family history, the SAA1 genotype, male gender, non-adherence to therapy, and national origin (paralleling infant mortality rate). Among the related syndromes, untreated TRAPS leads to amyloidosis in about 15% of cases, MWS in roughly 25%, while amyloidosis is uncommon in FCAS and is a late complication in NOMID. PFAPA generally has a benign course with resolution by early adulthood. NOMID is the most severe cryopyrinopathy.
pitfalls: A positive family history can be elicited in only about half of cases (especially where families are small), so its absence does not exclude FMF; FMF can also occur without known Mediterranean ancestry.

Only about 70% of clinically typical FMF patients carry two identifiable MEFV mutations in trans, and many clinical cases have only a single demonstrable mutation, so genetic testing cannot rule out the diagnosis.

Certain variants are functional polymorphisms rather than disease-causing: E148Q (common in some Asian populations) often affects overall inflammation more than causing clinical FMF, and TNFRSF1A R92Q and P46L may behave as polymorphisms in TRAPS.

Serum IgD elevation is neither sensitive nor specific for HIDS/MKD: disease activity does not track IgD levels, some FMF/TRAPS patients have modestly raised IgD, and some MVK-mutation patients have normal IgD (markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks is more reliable).
About one-third of NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations and require testing for somatic mosaicism, which can be missed on standard germline sequencing.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal numeric severity scale is given; the hereditary recurrent fevers are clinically stratified by syndrome (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, and the NLRP3-associated spectrum of FCAS [mildest] -> MWS -> NOMID [most severe]) and by attack length, organ involvement, and genotype. In FMF, M694V homozygosity marks more severe disease (earlier onset; higher frequency of arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis). Development of systemic AA amyloidosis defines the severe end of the disease spectrum.
management: Use colchicine as first-line therapy for familial Mediterranean fever to abort attacks and prevent AA amyloidosis
Deploy interleukin-1 blockade (anakinra or canakinumab) for colchicine-resistant FMF and as the mainstay for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes and mevalonate kinase deficiency
For TRAPS, treat acute attacks with corticosteroids and use interleukin-1 blockade for prophylaxis, with TNF inhibition (etanercept) as an alternative
Control acute febrile and serosal attacks symptomatically while avoiding unnecessary surgery for sterile peritonitis
Surveil for AA amyloidosis with urinalysis for proteinuria and acute-phase reactants, with renal biopsy when proteinuria is persistent
Direct diagnosis and targeted biologic selection by genotype across MEFV, TNFRSF1A, MVK and NLRP3
Provide genetic counselling and family screening with multidisciplinary rheumatology and nephrology follow-up
